projects.title: Which optimization actually shortens a small training run?
projects.summary: Use a profiler to identify the bottleneck, then test one optimization including its setup cost.
projects.question: When do faster attention or graph compilation repay their overhead in the short training runs a student actually performs?
projects.scope: Use a 5M-20M decoder, one fixed input batch stream, and two sequence lengths. Profile a baseline, then choose either supported optimized attention or graph compilation. Compare runs of 20, 100, and 500 steps on one GPU; check the installed backend supports the chosen method.
projects.baseline: Unoptimized execution with identical weights, batches, precision, optimizer, and hardware. Check outputs and gradients within documented numerical tolerances, and compare short loss trajectories before interpreting speed.
projects.evaluation: End-to-end elapsed time including compilation, steady-state tokens/second, peak allocated memory, repeated-run variation, and time spent in attention, optimizer, and data loading. Synchronize accelerator timing and separate warm-up from measurement.
projects.outcome: A profiler-backed bottleneck diagnosis, a correctness-checked change, and a break-even estimate showing when it helps or fails.
projects.preparation: PyTorch training and tensor shapes; learn profiling, asynchronous GPU timing, warm-up effects, and numerical equivalence checks.
projects.fallback: Use the smaller model and one sequence length. If GPU kernels are unavailable, analyze CPU execution and one supported optimization; do not report it as a GPU speedup. Distributed training and writing a Triton kernel are outside the minimum scope.

reading_notes.cs336-systems: Plan profiling, correctness checks, and fair timing.
reading_notes.torch-compile: Measure compilation overhead using the installed backend.

resources.note: One GPU, one optimization, and a fixed set of short step counts. Include compilation and profiling in the total; no distributed training or custom kernel is needed.

projects.title: When should a coding assistant ask a question first?
projects.summary: Measure the value and cost of one clarification on an underspecified programming request.
projects.question: Can a small model recognize missing requirements and ask a useful question without burdening users whose requests are already clear?
projects.scope: Author 40 small Python tasks with hidden specification fields such as tie-breaking, units, or case handling. Create paired complete and incomplete requests. Use a deterministic simulated user that reveals only the field explicitly requested, and allow at most one clarification.
projects.baseline: Answer immediately, always ask a fixed question, selectively ask, and an oracle given the full specification. Use the same model and total generation-token cap. Keep development templates separate from evaluation tasks and run code in a sandbox.
projects.evaluation: Hidden-test pass rate, useful and unnecessary question rates, unresolved ambiguities, interaction count, and total tokens. Inspect whether questions reveal task requirements rather than reference implementations.
projects.outcome: A paired task generator, a reproducible clarification policy comparison, and an analysis of when the additional interaction earns its cost.
projects.preparation: Python tests, basic prompting, and evaluation; learn controlled user simulation and ambiguity annotation. The CS224N gallery supplies topic inspiration; this is an original reduced protocol.
projects.fallback: Use 20 tasks, two ambiguity types, and a 0.6B model. Human user studies, unrestricted dialogue, and a full replication of the Stanford project are outside the minimum scope.

projects.title: Propose your own NLP or LLM project
projects.summary: Start with a topic you care about: a hobby, language, research question, community, or practical problem. The suggested projects are starting points, and you are welcome to propose a different idea.
projects.question: Which specific question about language processing would you be excited to investigate, and what evidence would change your mind?
projects.scope: Choose one question with a clear NLP or LLM component that one student can investigate this semester. Explain its motivation and connection to related work, identify accessible data or a small generator, and define one main comparison. For example, study terminology preservation in translations, search over historical documents, or a language tool for a hobby you know well.
projects.baseline: Begin with the simplest credible solution: a rule, majority prediction, lexical retrieval, or an existing small model. Identify one change to compare against it, and explain which outcome would support or weaken your hypothesis.
projects.evaluation: Define a held-out set, relevant quantitative or qualitative criteria, a baseline comparison, and an error analysis. Implement and test the proposed method, system, or audit; a literature survey or app demonstration alone is insufficient. Record the time and resources used.
projects.outcome: An individual investigation with a reproducible implementation or tested artifact, a meaningful comparison, and a clear explanation of findings and limitations. A well-supported negative result is valid and uses the same course rubric as a listed topic.
projects.preparation: Use the one-page proposal to cover motivation, related work, approach and baseline, data access, evaluation, compute, tools, and a short schedule. Identify what you will implement and what you will reuse, including AI coding assistance. Plan an early baseline and reserve time for analysis and writing. Connect your question to relevant prior work; the links below provide planning guidance.
projects.fallback: Narrow to one language, one dataset, fewer examples, or a smaller model if data or compute access is uncertain. Discuss feasibility with the instructor through the normal proposal feedback process. Submit the proposal by October 21; the final report has up to six pages of main content, excluding references and appendices.
projects.upstream: A custom project may also produce an upstream contribution if it meets a real maintainer need. Document its review or acceptance status; the same course rubric and maximum score apply, with no merge requirement or extra-credit track.

reading_notes.course-project: Follow this course’s individual scope, checkpoints, and rubric.

resources.note: Propose CPU, one-GPU, or two-GPU use and distinguish necessary devices from optional parallel runs. Larger setups are possible with resources you can obtain yourself. State the source, access, and total cost of all baselines, ablations, and reruns; scope any request to the small course pool separately. The displayed budget is an initial shared-pool planning target.
resources.note_zh: 请说明 CPU、单卡、双卡或更大配置，并区分必需设备与可选并行计算。若使用自有资源，请记录来源、可用性以及所有基线、消融和重跑的总成本；课程池申请单独列出。
